---
title: "Figure 16.2: LAC: Composition of FDI Capital Expenditure"
---

![Python: `python/fig-16-2.py`](../images/python/fig-16-2.png)

Annual FDI capital expenditure announced in the region, split by sector, as
stacked bars. The height of each bar is the total for the year; the
coloured segments show how much of it went to manufacturing, mining, ICT,
business services and other sectors.

**A clean example of stacked bars** on a year axis. Compare it with
[Figure 2.3](fig-2-3.qmd), which adds dots and a reordered legend, and with
[Figure 7.2](fig-7-2.qmd), which stacks positive and negative values.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 13 rows (2013 to 2025):

| category | Manufacturing | Mining | ICT and data | Business services | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2013 | 80.9 | 48.2 | 2.4 | 5.2 | 34.2 |

One column per sector, in billions of US dollars. All values are positive,
which keeps the stacking simple: each segment starts where the previous one
ended. There is no total column; the bar height is simply the sum of the
segments.

## The script

### The stacking order

```python
data = read_chart_data(STEM)
years = data["category"]

# Stacking order, from the bottom up, and colours.
sector_colours = {
    "Manufacturing": "#5B2A7E",
    "Mining": "#C75B12",
    "ICT and data": "#00649A",
    "Business services": "#009A9A",
    "Other": "#B8BCBE",
}
```

The dictionary does two jobs. It links each sector to its colour, and its
order is the stacking order, from the bottom up. Manufacturing, the largest
sector, sits at the bottom, as in the published chart. "Other" is grey and
on top: a residual category is usually drawn in a neutral colour so that the
eye goes to the named sectors.

In Python, a dictionary keeps the order in which its entries were written,
so the loop below always runs through the sectors in this order.

### The stack

```python
bottom = np.zeros(len(data))
for sector, colour in sector_colours.items():
    ax.bar(years, data[sector], bottom=bottom, width=0.56, color=colour,
           label=sector)
    bottom += data[sector].to_numpy()
```

matplotlib has no "stacked bar chart" type, as Excel does. Instead,
`ax.bar()` takes a `bottom` argument: the height at which each bar starts.
Stacking is then a loop with a running total:

1. `bottom` starts as 13 zeros, one per year (`np.zeros(len(data))`).
2. The first sector, Manufacturing, is drawn from zero.
3. Its values are added to `bottom`, so `bottom` now holds the top of the
   Manufacturing segments.
4. Mining is drawn starting from there, and added in turn, and so on up the
   stack.

`data[sector].to_numpy()` turns the pandas column into a plain array of
numbers before adding it. That way the addition is position by position, and
pandas does not try to match row labels. See [Stacked
bars](../techniques.qmd#sec-stacked).

Because the years are numbers, the bars are drawn directly at the years:
there is no need for positions 0, 1, 2, .... On a year axis, `width=0.56`
means 0.56 of a year, so bars fill a little more than half the space and
the gaps a little less.

`label=sector` stores each sector's name for the legend.

### The axes

```python
ax.set_xlim(2012.5, 2025.5)
ax.set_xticks(range(2013, 2026, 2))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=2.8, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, 0, 300, 60)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)
```

- **The x-limits** are half a year beyond the first and last bars, so every
  bar has the same space around it.
- **Labels** go on every second year: `range(2013, 2026, 2)` gives 2013,
  2015, ..., 2025. The other years have no tick mark.
- **The y-axis** runs from 0 to 300 in steps of 60. That is an unusual step,
  but it gives six labelled intervals, which is what the published chart
  uses. See [The y-scale](../chart-style.qmd#sec-y-scale).

### The legend

```python
ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.04, 1.0), handlelength=0.9,
          handleheight=0.9, handletextpad=0.4, labelspacing=0.15)
```

For bars, the legend shows a filled box in each colour. By default the box
is a wide rectangle. `handlelength=0.9` and `handleheight=0.9` make it a
small square, as in the published chart. Both are in units of the font
size. `handletextpad=0.4` brings the text closer to the square, and
`labelspacing=0.15` keeps the five entries close together.

The legend lists the sectors in drawing order, so Manufacturing, the bottom
of the stack, comes first. That matches the published chart here, but it is
the reverse of what the eye sees, since Manufacturing is at the bottom of
the bars and the top of the legend. In [Figure 7.2](fig-7-2.qmd) the legend
is reversed to follow the stack from the top. See
[Legends](../techniques.qmd#sec-legends).

## Changing the chart

- **A different stacking order.** Reorder the entries of `sector_colours`.
  The bars and the legend both follow.
- **Reverse the legend** to match the stack visually:

  ```python
  handles, labels = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
  ax.legend(handles[::-1], labels[::-1], loc="upper left", ...)
  ```

- **Shares instead of levels.** Divide each row by its total before
  drawing, `data[list(sector_colours)].div(data[list(sector_colours)].sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100`,
  and set the y-scale to 0–100.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-16-2.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-16-2.py"}
"""Figure 16.2: LAC: Composition of FDI Capital Expenditure."""
import numpy as np

from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart, set_y_scale

STEM = "fig-16-2"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)
years = data["category"]

# Stacking order, from the bottom up, and colours.
sector_colours = {
    "Manufacturing": "#5B2A7E",
    "Mining": "#C75B12",
    "ICT and data": "#00649A",
    "Business services": "#009A9A",
    "Other": "#B8BCBE",
}

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="LAC: Composition of FDI Capital Expenditure",
    subtitle="(Billions of US dollars; annual levels)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: Orbis Crossborder Investment database; and IMF staff\n"
        "calculations.\n"
        "Note: Years are announcement years and cover announced and\n"
        "completed projects. Latest available data as of September 2, 2026. FDI =\n"
        "foreign direct investments; ICT = information and communications\n"
        "technology and data; LAC = Latin America and the Caribbean."
    ),
    left=0.35,
    right=0.15,
    bottom_gap=0.3,
)

bottom = np.zeros(len(data))
for sector, colour in sector_colours.items():
    ax.bar(years, data[sector], bottom=bottom, width=0.56, color=colour,
           label=sector)
    bottom += data[sector].to_numpy()

ax.set_xlim(2012.5, 2025.5)
ax.set_xticks(range(2013, 2026, 2))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=2.8, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, 0, 300, 60)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)

ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.04, 1.0), handlelength=0.9,
          handleheight=0.9, handletextpad=0.4, labelspacing=0.15)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
